summary: Help 6–7 year-olds understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem: 12 − 9 = ? asks the same question as 9 + ? = 12 — find the missing PART of a known whole. Anchor the equivalence on a part-whole model, teach counting up from the subtrahend when the numbers are close, and repeatedly pair each subtraction with its addition twin. A linked part-whole/number-line display can make the 'same gap, two routes' insight concrete; dialogue draws out the justification; matching and missing-number tasks consolidate; a static part-whole picture (with a double ten-frame and fact-family triangle as further representations) anchors both equations against one diagram.
misconceptions: Believing subtraction can only mean 'take away / count back', so refusing to count up.
Not seeing 8 + ? = 10 and 10 − 8 = ? as the same question.
Counting back inefficiently for close numbers (12−11 counted back eleven steps) and making errors.
Confusing which quantity is the whole and which is a part in the part-whole model.
Treating the answer to 8 + ? = 10 as 10 (writing the whole) rather than the missing part.

activities.title: Two routes, one gap: linked part-whole and number line
steps: Look at a part-whole bar with whole 10 and known part 8, and a number line beside it.
First try to count BACK from the whole by the known part (back 8 from 10) to find the missing part; notice this is fiddly for some pairs.
Then start at the known part (8) and hop UP to the whole (8→9→10), counting the jumps to find the gap.
See both routes highlight the SAME gap of 2, and read the two printed sentences 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10 together.
Repeat with a close-number case such as 12 − 9: count back nine steps, then instead start at 9 and hop up 9→10→11→12 (three easy jumps), and see 12 − 9 = 3 printed above 9 + 3 = 12.
activities.insight: A subtraction and its unknown-addend twin ask the same question — the missing part of a whole — and counting up from the subtrahend is often the shortcut, especially when the numbers are close.

activities.title: Explain why counting up works
steps: Solve a close-number subtraction such as 12 − 9 using whatever method you choose.
Answer aloud: 'You could take 9 away — but is there a quicker way to get from 9 up to 12?'
State the matching addition sentence (9 + ? = 12) for the subtraction.
Explain in your own words why 12 − 9 and 9 + ? = 12 are the same question.
activities.insight: Being able to justify the equivalence — not just produce the number — shows the child reads subtraction additively rather than only as take-away.

activities.title: Match, fill, and choose the quicker route
steps: Match each subtraction to its unknown-addend twin, e.g. 13 − 9 ↔ 9 + □ = 13.
Fill in the missing addend: 9 + □ = 13 (answer 4), then write the matching subtraction 13 − 9 = 4.
Decide which is quicker for 12 − 9 — counting up or counting back — and give a reason.
Given a known fact such as 8 + 5 = 13, write a subtraction you can now answer straight away.
activities.insight: Consolidate the pairing of subtraction with its addition twin and the strategic choice of counting up when numbers are close.

activities.title: One diagram, both equations (anchor)
steps: Look at a part-whole diagram with a tappable whole and one known part.
Tap or lift a flap to reveal the missing part.
Read both equation forms shown side by side against the same diagram, e.g. 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10.
Name which number is the whole and which are the parts.

Compare the same whole and parts in other representations — a ten-frame with 8 cells filled and the gap of 2 to ten visible (use a double ten-frame for wholes above 10, e.g. 9 filled plus 3 more to reach 12), and a fact-family triangle linking the whole and its two parts — and read how each shows the missing part.
activities.insight: Both the subtraction and its addition twin describe the same part-whole picture, and the answer is the missing part.

checkQuestion: Here is a subtraction: 12 − 9. Work out the answer. Then tell me how this is the same as the addition 9 + ? = 12.
checkAnswer: 3 — and explains that 12 − 9 asks the same question as 9 + ? = 12: the number you add to 9 to reach 12 is the same as the number left when you take 9 from 12, so both give 3. Often solved by counting up from 9.
